name: The Whistler Cork Oak (Sobreiro Assobiador)

location.address: Águas de Moura, Palmela municipality, Setubal District, Portugal (in the village streets, marked as 'Sobreiro Monumental')

access: Free, public, no barrier beyond a small protective fence around the trunk. Stands in the open in the village of Aguas de Moura, beside a playground, benches and a car park with an EV charging point; signposted in the streets. Nothing to book, nothing to ask permission for.
transport: In the village of Aguas de Moura itself, on foot from anywhere in the village centre; reachable from Setubal by the Carris Metropolitana 4540 bus (about 20km, roughly 39 minutes, hourly).
verify_notes: Confirmed winner of European Tree of the Year 2018 with 26,606 public votes (the inaugural year Portugal entered the competition, beating the runner-up, ancient elms of Cabeza del Buey in Spain, on 22,323 votes), and separately listed in the Guinness Book of Records as the largest cork oak in the world. This is one of the most-covered individual trees in Portuguese media (Observador, RTP, Publico all covered it) and carries genuine cross-border name recognition, unlike most of this project's leads. NAME: nicknamed 'Assobiador' (Whistler) for the birdsong of the many songbirds that gather in its crown at dusk. AGE: planting date of 1783-84 (reign of Queen Maria I) is a documented planting date for this specific tree, repeated identically by Wikipedia, treeoftheyear.org and the 2023 Portuguese press piece, so this is a genuine dated estimate rather than a vague one -- recorded as roughly 240 years (2026 minus 1783/84), kept to a narrow band since the planting date itself is specific even though the exact day is not. SIZE: trunk circumference is given as 4.15m at breast height by Wikipedia (recorded as girth_cm) and 'over 6m at the base' by a 2023 press account -- both plausible and not contradictory, cork oaks flare heavily at the base, so noted as two different measurement points rather than a conflict to resolve. Height 16.2m (Wikipedia) vs 19m (2023 press, describing a measurement 'from about 4 years prior') -- flagging the discrepancy for the writer rather than picking one. Crown diameter over 30m per the 2023 source. PRODUCTION: has been stripped of cork more than 20 times since roughly 1820; a single 1991 harvest yielded over 1,200kg of cork, reportedly enough for more than 100,000 wine-bottle stoppers, well above what an average cork oak produces in its whole life -- a good concrete fact for the story. DESIGNATION: classified 'Tree of Public Interest' since 1988 by what is now ICNF (Portugal's forestry institute), which is the custodian. HISTORY: in 2000 the tree faced a real threat from illegal urban expansion nearby; protective legislation around it was strengthened by 2001, and it has stood without incident since. ALIVE/CURRENT: a dated Portuguese press piece from 2023-09-05 describes it as actively cared for by the community ('they always take good care of it'), used daily for its shade by families with children on the benches beside it -- solid, fairly recent, first-hand confirmation. COORDINATES: two independent readings differ by several hundred metres (Wikipedia's infobox at 38.58667,-8.69111 vs treeoftheyear.org's 38.58889,-8.69651); the brief's own coordinate (38.58659,-8.69098, used here) sits within about 15m of Wikipedia's figure and is treated as the tree-level pin, with treeoftheyear.org's more distant figure noted as the likely less precise of the two. DESTINATION TEST: passes overwhelmingly -- this is arguably the single most internationally famous tree in this whole batch, with a Guinness record, a European popular vote win against entries from a dozen countries, and dedicated infrastructure (parking, EV charger, playground, signage) built around it as a visitor attraction in its own right. CONTAINER, a genuine judgment call for the orchestrating session: Aguas de Moura sits in Palmela municipality, roughly 20km / 39 minutes by an hourly direct bus from Setubal (already published, data/cities/setubal.json, 10 trees) -- just outside CLAUDE.md's 'roughly 30 minutes' day-trip boundary, and the village is not perceived as part of Setubal by anyone (different municipality, sits toward Alcacer do Sal/inland Alentejo rather than the Setubal peninsula). Given the borderline transit time and that the tree is already a nationally famous standalone attraction with its own identity, recommend publishing it as its own single-tree place ('Aguas de Moura') under the 2026-08-31 exception rather than folding it into Setubal, but flagging this explicitly since 39 minutes is close enough to the boundary that a case could be made either way.
